title: Minutes Battles to Watch
brief: Which players are in a fight for minutes or a starting job, and which battles matter for our auction prices? It must note the hedge option of buying both candidates cheaply and cutting the loser, and that a starting job alone does not guarantee minutes.
summary: A minutes battle cuts a player's auction price. That price drop is only value if you have a reason to think he wins the job. The cheap way to play a battle you cannot call is to buy both candidates at 1 to 2 USD in the endgame and cut the loser within the first two weeks. A starting job alone does not prove a player is worth his price, so judge every battle by minutes, not by who starts.

paragraphs.text: When some drafters think a player might lose his starting job or share minutes, his price drops. That drop is value only if you believe he keeps the role. Before you bid on a discounted player, write down why you think he wins. If you have no reason, do not treat the low price as a bargain.

Small losses count. Losing even two to three minutes a game limits a player's upside and lowers his draft value. If a player's price assumes a certain number of minutes, bid as if he loses a few of them. This matters most for mid-round buys at 10 USD or more, where you pay for a full role.

Crowded rosters shrink the pool. When a team has too many players at the same positions, the minutes get spread thin and fewer of those players are worth drafting. Coaches do not play 12 or more players, so some good players lose time unless injuries open it up. Our draft takes 144 players. Do not assume every rotation player from a crowded team belongs in that pool. Project the rotation first, then bid.

sections.heading: A starting job does not guarantee minutes

paragraphs.text: Minutes can matter more than a starting spot. A bench player can play about as many minutes as a nominal starter. Winning the start is not enough to make a player worth his price, and losing it does not always make him worthless.

For our league, check minutes per game in the box scores, not just the starting lineup. In the first two weeks, compare the two candidates' minutes and see who is on the floor late in games. If the starter gets two to three fewer minutes than his price assumed, his value has dropped even though he kept the job.

sections.heading: The hedge: buy both, cut the loser

paragraphs.text: Two notes describe the same hedge. Draft both players fighting for one starting job or one set of minutes. See which one wins the role, then drop the other.

One note frames this as a late-draft move. In our auction, that means the endgame, near the 144-player cutoff, where each candidate costs about 1 to 2 USD. Paying two mid-round prices for one job wastes auction dollars. Save the hedge for battles where both players are cheap.

The hedge costs roster spots. We draft 12 players with only 2 bench slots, so one hedge pair can fill your whole bench. Plan for that before the endgame starts, and do not run more than one pair unless one of the players fills a Util slot.

Cut fast. Waivers process daily, and dropping the loser costs one of your 6 weekly adds. Once the minutes show who won, usually in the first two weeks, drop the loser for the best waiver option. Holding both all season wastes a roster spot.

sections.heading: Where the notes pull in different directions

paragraphs.text: The notes point two ways on discounted players. One note says that fear of a lost job lowers a player's price, which creates value if you think he starts. Other notes warn that crowded rosters spread minutes thin, that not every good player gets time, and that you should project the rotation before you reach for anyone. In practice: buy the discount when you can project the rotation and he comes out ahead. When you cannot call the battle, hedge cheaply in the endgame or leave both players for waivers.

sections.heading: What to check after the draft

paragraphs.text: For every battle on your roster, track starts, minutes per game and who closes games in the first two weeks. Measure each player against the minutes his price assumed, because losing two to three minutes lowers his value. Act on what you see before the battle is fully settled in the box scores. Other managers watch the same numbers.

Keep a watch list of the players who lost their battles. On crowded rosters, injuries are what open up minutes. When a starter goes down, the loser of a battle can become a FAB add overnight. This stays true through the 2027-03-04 trade deadline and into our playoff weeks, which end on 2027-03-28.
